title: After Trump’s Russian diesel deal, will Europe give Ukraine the support it needs?
gist: Chatham House argues that Trump's Russian diesel deal is a distraction from Russia's shift to a missile-and-drone campaign aimed at breaking Ukraine's economy, which is widening a financing gap of $27bn (2026) and $32bn (2027) and threatens IMF disbursements. It urges Europe to seize the €210bn of frozen Russian central bank assets via an EU SPV and to build first-loss and expanded URGF insurance schemes to protect Ukraine's productive assets and $10-11bn grain export trade.

themes.theme: Trump's Russian diesel deal and US-Kyiv rift

insights.claim: President Trump struck a deal with Moscow that could release millions of barrels of Russian diesel to global markets, openly framed as lowering prices for Americans ahead of the November 2026 midterms.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US domestic fuel-price politics is now directly shaping Russia sanctions policy, adding diesel supply and loosening pressure on Moscow's revenues.
insights.quote: which could see millions of barrels of Russian diesel released to global markets
insights.locator: An intervention by President Donald Trump

insights.claim: Chatham House doubts the Russian diesel deal will meaningfully swing midterm votes toward Trump's party, but says it has opened another public dispute between Trump and Zelenskyy when Ukraine most needs focused allied support.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The political payoff is weak while the diplomatic cost to Ukraine is real, raising the onus on Europe.
insights.quote: It is uncertain that the deal will do much to swing votes back to the president
insights.locator: It is uncertain that the deal

insights.claim: Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy grid have continued and extended to transmission infrastructure despite the 'energy ceasefire' Trump claimed was part of his deal with Moscow.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US-brokered assurances with Moscow are not being honoured, undermining their credibility as a basis for policy.
insights.locator: And attacks have continued on Ukraine’s energy grid

insights.claim: Chatham House argues that Trump's deal with Putin undermines Ukraine but will not fundamentally change the war; the decisive factor is getting Ukraine's economy through the winter.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Markets should focus on Ukraine's economic resilience and European financing rather than headline US-Russia deals.
insights.quote: Trump’s deal with Putin undermines Ukraine, but it will not fundamentally change the war situation.
insights.locator: Trump’s deal with Putin undermines Ukraine

insights.claim: Rather than ordering a new mobilization wave and a Donbas offensive as some expected, Putin has intensified ballistic missile and drone strikes aimed at breaking Ukraine's economy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The war's centre of gravity is shifting from front lines to economic infrastructure, raising Ukraine's fiscal needs.
insights.quote: Instead, he has moved to intensify Russia’s ballistic missile and drone campaign, with the aim of breaking Ukraine’s economy.
insights.locator: Recent weeks have seen a noticeable shift

insights.claim: Russia has sharply increased attacks on Ukrainian ports, grain storage and shipping, apparently to block agricultural exports, and has also hit Dnipro bridges in Kyiv, railways nationwide, retail, warehousing and logistics hubs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ukraine's export logistics chain, especially grain, is under direct threat, with implications for global grain supply and Ukraine's FX earnings.
insights.quote: There has been a marked uptick in attacks on ports, grain storage and shipping
insights.locator: There has been a marked uptick

insights.claim: Russian strikes on Ukraine's steel plants have put five blast furnaces permanently out of action.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Permanent loss of metallurgical capacity cuts Ukraine's industrial output and export revenues for the long term.
insights.quote: strikes on Ukraine’s steel plants have put five blast furnaces permanently out of action
insights.locator: Meanwhile, strikes on Ukraine’s steel plants

insights.claim: Russia's aim is to push Ukraine's economy back into recession, cause hardship, erode morale, and possibly trigger a new migration crisis out of the country.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A renewed Ukrainian refugee outflow would add fiscal and political strain on EU host countries.
insights.quote: It may even hope to spark a new migration crisis out of the country.
insights.locator: Russia’s intention is to tip

insights.claim: Putin's strategy is to raise the cost of supporting Ukraine while Europe's public finances are weak and anti-Ukraine-funding far-right parties are rising, ahead of key elections such as France's in May 2027, so Ukraine's cause looks hopeless and unaffordable.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: European election outcomes, especially France, are a key risk to the durability of Ukraine financing.
insights.quote: With key elections looming, particularly in France next May
insights.locator: Putin’s strategy is clear.

themes.theme: Ukraine's financing gap and IMF risk

insights.claim: Ukraine was already warning of a $27 billion defence financing gap in 2026 and a $32 billion budget financing shortfall in 2027, before the latest escalation of Russian economic attacks.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ukraine's external financing needs are large and growing, putting pressure on European budgets and donors.
insights.quote: Ukraine was already warning of a $27 billion defence financing gap in 2026 and a budget financing shortfall of $32 billion in 2027.
insights.locator: That is a serious problem.

insights.claim: The IMF will likely stall further disbursements under Ukraine's $7 billion Extended Financing Facility unless the financing gap is closed or new financing assurances are provided.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: An IMF programme stall would be a negative signal for Ukraine's sovereign credit and could trigger other donors' conditionality.
insights.quote: the IMF will likely stall further disbursements under Ukraine’s $7 billion Extended Financing Facility (EFF)
insights.locator: The problems are so acute

insights.claim: Stagnating GDP, stalling revenues and a widening budget deficit, worsened by Russian strikes and a longer war, will raise Ukraine's financing ask of its European allies.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Ukraine's fiscal needs scale with the intensity and length of the war, making European funding commitments open-ended.
insights.locator: Wreaking havoc on Ukraine’s budget

themes.theme: Seizing frozen Russian central bank assets

insights.claim: Chatham House says the $90 billion Ukraine Support Loan agreed at the December 2025 EU Council could be increased, as part of a European 'financial bazooka' sending Putin a message that Europe is committed for the long haul regardless of Trump.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A larger EU loan would mean more joint EU borrowing or budget commitments in support of Ukraine.
insights.quote: the $90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL) agreed at the EU Council meeting in December 2025 could be increased
insights.locator: To begin, the $90 billion

insights.claim: The preferred option is for Europe to seize the €210 billion of immobilized Russian Central Bank assets held in the EU, mostly in Belgium, plus €25 billion in the UK, so Russia rather than European taxpayers pays for the war.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Asset seizure would shift Ukraine's funding burden off European budgets but carries legal and reserve-currency risk; watch the Brussels summit.
insights.quote: seize the €210 billion of immobilized Russia Central Bank (CBR) assets in the EU (mostly in Belgium) and €25 billion in the UK

insights.claim: To overcome Belgium's resistance, the frozen assets should be moved out of Belgian jurisdiction into a common EU-managed Special Purpose Vehicle, with the wider European community indemnifying Belgium's legal risks, and then invested for higher returns to fund larger Extraordinary Revenue Arrangement-style facilities.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A mutualized SPV structure is the likely path to unlock the assets and would concentrate legal exposure at EU level rather than in Euroclear's home country.
insights.quote: First, the assets should be taken out of Belgium’s jurisdiction to a common EU managed Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV).
insights.locator: The Belgian government, which has resisted

insights.claim: Chatham House argues that the security imperative should override legal and economic objections to seizing Russian assets, and that Belgium should not have a veto on European security.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals rising policy pressure to prioritize security over legal norms on sovereign asset immunity.
insights.locator: Ultimately the security imperative should prevail

themes.theme: Insuring and rebuilding Ukraine's productive base

insights.claim: More and better air defences are the obvious military fix for Russian strikes on Ukraine's economy, but they are in short supply because of President Trump's war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Competing demand from the Iran war tightens global air-defence supply, leaving Ukraine's infrastructure more exposed.
insights.quote: But these are in short supply as a result of President Trump’s war with Iran.
insights.locator: Urgent measures are also needed

insights.claim: A first-loss compensation scheme, in which the Ukrainian government and donors cover first losses from attacks on productive assets, would make private insurers more willing to provide war-risk cover and enable fast reconstruction of factories, farms, energy and logistics assets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Blended-finance de-risking could keep private capital and insurance in Ukraine; without it, existing limited cover may be withdrawn.
insights.quote: if the Ukrainian government and international donors offer to cover the first losses from attacks on Ukrainian productive assets, private insurers will be more likely to commit
insights.locator: But if the Ukrainian government

insights.claim: The EBRD-backed Ukrainian Recovery and Reconstruction Guarantee Facility (URGF), used to insure agricultural exports, is capped at €2 million per shipment and €5 million per client, covers only 60 days of transit on a Free on Board basis, and excludes storage, leaving grain in ports and silos uninsured where Russia is now attacking.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
insights.so_what: The coverage gap matches exactly where Russia is striking, so extending URGF to port terminal storage is a concrete policy lever to watch.
insights.quote: But its cover is limited in size to €2million per shipment and €5 million per client.

insights.claim: Grain exports earn Ukraine $10-11 billion a year, so donors must make shipping from Ukrainian ports financially viable again, for example by expanding URGF scale and scope to cover port terminal storage.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Protecting grain exports is critical to Ukraine's FX earnings and to global grain markets.
insights.quote: Grain exports earn between $10-11 billion annually for Ukraine.

insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: NATO cover for Black Sea shipping would be a major escalation option with implications for shipping insurance and grain prices.
